overview: Object-oriented design in Python models data and behavior together using classes, where __init__ initializes instance state and self refers to the specific instance.

Classes support instance vs class attributes, three method kinds (instance, @classmethod, @staticmethod), inheritance with super(), dunder methods like __repr__ and __eq__, and @property for computed/validated attributes.
Modern Python favors @dataclass to remove boilerplate and prefers composition over inheritance for flexible, maintainable designs - all central to writing clean, testable data-engineering code.
learningObjectives: Understand how classes, __init__, self, and instance vs class attributes define object state and behavior.
Master inheritance with super(), the distinction between @classmethod and @staticmethod, and dunder methods like __repr__/__eq__ and @property.
Apply @dataclass to reduce boilerplate and choose between composition and inheritance for robust designs.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A class is a blueprint that defines a new type by bundling state (attributes) and behavior (methods). An instance is a concrete object created from the class; __init__ is the initializer invoked after instance creation to set up instance attributes, where self is the conventional first parameter bound to the instance. Python's object model supports single and multiple inheritance resolved via the C3 linearization (MRO) and customizable behavior through special 'dunder' methods.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: A class is like a cookie cutter and instances are the cookies. The cutter (class) defines the shape and what features every cookie has; each cookie (instance) can have its own decorations (instance attributes). 'self' is how a cookie refers to itself when you ask it to describe its own decorations.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Object orientation traces to Simula (1960s) and Smalltalk (1970s). Python has been object-oriented since its 1991 creation, where 'everything is an object'. Python 3 unified old- and new-style classes under a single object model. Properties (descriptors) were formalized early, and @dataclass (PEP 557) arrived in Python 3.7 to standardize boilerplate-free data classes inspired by attrs.

whyItMatters.business: Well-designed classes model domain concepts (Customer, Pipeline, Dataset) clearly, making systems easier to extend as business requirements change and reducing the cost of new features.
whyItMatters.engineering: Encapsulation and clear interfaces let teams reason about components independently, test in isolation, and swap implementations without breaking callers.
whyItMatters.scalability: Composition and small, focused classes scale better than deep inheritance trees; clean abstractions allow components (sources, sinks, transforms) to be combined and parallelized.
whyItMatters.cost: Boilerplate-free dataclasses and reusable base classes reduce development time and bugs; good design lowers long-term maintenance cost far more than micro-optimizations.
whyItMatters.reliability: Properties enforce invariants and validation, __eq__/__repr__ make objects debuggable and testable, and immutability (frozen dataclasses) prevents accidental state corruption.

coreComponents.name: Class, __init__, and self
coreComponents.definition: A class defines a type; __init__ is the initializer that sets up instance attributes; self is the instance the method operates on.
coreComponents.purpose: To create objects with their own state and to access that state inside methods.
coreComponents.responsibilities: __init__ assigns instance attributes; every instance method takes self as its first parameter to read/write that instance's data.
coreComponents.examples: class Dataset:\n    def __init__(self, name):\n        self.name = name

coreComponents.name: Instance vs class attributes
coreComponents.definition: Instance attributes are unique per object (set on self); class attributes are shared by all instances (defined in the class body).
coreComponents.purpose: Instance attributes hold per-object state; class attributes hold shared constants or defaults.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Avoid mutable class attributes as defaults (shared mutation bug); use them for constants like a version or a registry.

coreComponents.name: Methods: instance, @classmethod, @staticmethod
coreComponents.definition: Instance methods take self; classmethods take cls and operate on the class; staticmethods take neither and are namespaced utilities.
coreComponents.purpose: Instance methods act on object state; classmethods are alternative constructors/factories; staticmethods group related functions.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Use @classmethod for factories (from_dict) that may respect subclasses via cls; use @staticmethod for pure helpers that need no class/instance state.

internalWorking: Calling ClassName(args) invokes the metaclass __call__, which calls __new__ to allocate the instance, then __init__ to initialize it; the returned object's attributes live in its __dict__ (unless __slots__ is used).

Attribute lookup follows the MRO (method resolution order): Python checks the instance __dict__ first, then the class and its bases in C3-linearized order, invoking descriptors like properties along the way.

super() returns a proxy that dispatches method calls to the next class in the MRO, enabling cooperative multiple inheritance; dunder methods are looked up on the type, not the instance, which is why operators like == call __eq__ on the class.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: ClassName(args) -> __new__ (allocate) -> __init__ (initialize state via self) -> instance ; method call -> MRO lookup -> bound method(self/cls)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A pipeline creates job = ETLJob.from_config(cfg) using a @classmethod factory.
2. from_config parses cfg and calls cls(**kwargs), so __new__ allocates and __init__ sets self.source, self.sink.
3. job.run() looks up 'run' via the MRO (ETLJob then its base), binding self, and executes the transform.
4. print(job) triggers __repr__ on the class, producing a readable, debuggable representation for logs.

keyTerminology.meaning: The conventional name for the first parameter of an instance method, automatically bound to the instance the method is called on.
keyTerminology.importance: It is how methods read and modify per-instance state; misunderstanding self is a top source of beginner bugs.

keyTerminology.meaning: The deterministic order, computed by C3 linearization, in which Python searches base classes for attributes and methods.
keyTerminology.importance: Determines which method runs under inheritance and how super() cooperates in multiple inheritance.

keyTerminology.meaning: Methods with double underscores (e.g., __init__, __repr__, __eq__) that hook into Python language operations and built-in functions.
keyTerminology.importance: They let your objects integrate with operators, printing, comparisons, and containers like first-class types.

importantConcepts.explanation: A @classmethod receives the class as cls and is ideal for alternative constructors (from_dict, from_json) because cls respects subclassing. A @staticmethod receives neither self nor cls - it's just a function logically grouped in the class namespace, used for pure utilities that need no instance or class state.

@property turns a method into a read-only attribute accessed without parentheses; pairing it with a @x.setter adds validation on assignment. It lets you expose a clean attribute interface while keeping logic behind it (e.g., validate a non-negative row count).

The @dataclass decorator auto-generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ from annotated class fields, removing boilerplate. Options include frozen=True (immutable, hashable), order=True (comparison methods), and field(default_factory=list) to safely default mutable types.

variationsAndTypes: **Regular classes:** Full control with explicit __init__ and methods; best when behavior is complex.
**Dataclasses:** Boilerplate-free data containers; frozen dataclasses give immutable, hashable value objects.
**Abstract base classes (abc.ABC):** Define interfaces with @abstractmethod that subclasses must implement, useful for plugin-style source/sink contracts.
**NamedTuple / TypedDict:** Lightweight immutable records and typed dict shapes when a full class is overkill.
advantages: **Encapsulation:** Bundles state and behavior, hiding internals behind a clean interface.
**Reusability:** Inheritance and composition let you reuse and extend code.
**Polymorphism:** Common interfaces (duck typing or ABCs) let different implementations be used interchangeably.
disadvantages: **Over-engineering risk:** Deep inheritance hierarchies become rigid and hard to follow.
**Hidden state:** Mutable shared state (class attributes, aliasing) can cause subtle bugs.
**Overhead vs simple data:** A full class can be heavier than a dict/tuple when you only need a record.
**MRO complexity:** Multiple inheritance and super() chains can be hard to reason about if misused.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use classes when you have state plus behavior that belong together, need polymorphism, or want to enforce invariants. Use dataclasses for structured records and composition to assemble behaviors flexibly.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid creating classes for pure stateless functions (just use functions/modules), avoid deep inheritance when composition fits, and avoid full classes when a NamedTuple, dict, or dataclass would suffice.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Think of building with LEGO. A class is a type of brick with defined studs (its interface). Inheritance is making a special brick that's a kind of the original. Composition is snapping several different bricks together to build a car - the car isn't a kind of wheel or a kind of engine; it has them. Good designs, like good LEGO models, favor combining simple pieces (composition) over creating one giant specialized brick (deep inheritance).

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should use inheritance whenever two classes share code.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Sharing code is not an 'is-a' relationship. Inheritance should model genuine subtype relationships; for mere code reuse, composition (has-a) is usually more flexible and avoids the fragile base class problem.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A mutable default like a list can be safely used as a class attribute or default argument.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A single mutable object is shared across all instances/calls, so mutations leak between them. Use None defaults plus initialization in __init__, or field(default_factory=list) in a dataclass.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Prefer small, composable classes and clear interfaces (ABCs/protocols) so components like sources, transforms, and sinks can be combined and parallelized without rewrites; use __slots__ for memory efficiency when creating millions of instances.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Enforce invariants in __init__ and property setters, prefer frozen dataclasses for value objects to prevent accidental mutation, and implement __eq__/__hash__ consistently so objects behave correctly in sets and dict keys.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Keep object construction side-effect-free (validate, don't perform I/O in __init__) so failures are isolated and objects are easy to recreate; use factory classmethods that can fail cleanly.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Implement informative __repr__ so logs and tracebacks show object state; avoid leaking secrets in __repr__ by overriding it for sensitive fields.
productionConsiderations.security: Don't expose internal mutable state directly; use properties to validate inputs, and override __repr__ to redact credentials (e.g., a Config object should not print its password).
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Use dataclasses and __slots__ to reduce per-instance memory; avoid unnecessary object churn in hot loops by reusing or using lightweight tuples/namedtuples.
productionConsiderations.performance: Attribute access via properties and deep MRO chains adds overhead; for hot paths, prefer plain attributes, __slots__, and shallow hierarchies. Dataclasses generate efficient code comparable to hand-written classes.

codeExamples.title: Class basics: __init__, self, instance vs class attributes, methods
codeExamples.overview: Defines an ETLJob with instance and class attributes and the three method kinds, illustrating self, cls, and a static utility.
codeExamples.breakdown: default_retries is a class attribute shared by all instances. __init__ sets per-instance name/source via self. describe() is an instance method using self. from_config is a @classmethod factory using cls (so subclasses build the right type). is_valid_source is a @staticmethod utility needing no state.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting self as the first parameter, or referencing default_retries without ETLJob/self prefix. Mutating a mutable class attribute affects all instances.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use cls (not the hardcoded class name) inside classmethods so subclasses work correctly. Add __slots__ if you create many instances and want lower memory.

codeExamples.title: Inheritance, super(), and dunder methods (__repr__, __eq__)
codeExamples.overview: Shows a base/subclass relationship with cooperative super(), plus __repr__ and __eq__ for debuggable, comparable objects.
codeExamples.breakdown: S3Source inherits from DataSource and calls super().__init__(uri) to run the base initializer before adding its own region attribute. __repr__ uses type(self).__name__ so subclasses print their own name. __eq__ compares by uri and returns NotImplemented for unrelated types (the correct protocol).
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting super().__init__ leaves base attributes unset. Returning False instead of NotImplemented for foreign types breaks reflected comparisons. Defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes the object unhashable (set __hash__ if needed).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: If you define __eq__ and want the object hashable, also define __hash__ consistently (or use a frozen dataclass). Use type(self).__name__ in __repr__ for subclass-friendly output.

codeExamples.title: @property validation and @dataclass (composition over inheritance)
codeExamples.overview: Uses @property with a setter for validation, and a frozen @dataclass as an immutable value object composed into a larger class.
codeExamples.breakdown: @dataclass(frozen=True) auto-generates __init__/__repr__/__eq__ and makes TableSchema immutable and hashable; default_factory=list avoids the shared-mutable-default bug. Table composes a TableSchema (has-a) rather than inheriting. row_count is exposed as a property whose setter validates non-negativity.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using 'columns: list = []' (without default_factory) shares one list across all instances. Assigning a negative row_count raises ValueError. Trying to mutate a frozen dataclass field raises FrozenInstanceError.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use frozen dataclasses for value objects you put in sets/dict keys (they're hashable). Prefer composition (Table has-a TableSchema) over inheritance for flexibility and easier testing.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A data platform needs a configurable ETL framework where many pipelines share common run/logging behavior but differ in their source, transform, and sink. The design must be easy to extend with new sources without rewriting existing code, validate configuration, and produce debuggable, comparable objects.
endToEndExample.inputData: Pipeline configuration dictionaries specifying a source type (s3, postgres), transform parameters, and a destination table, plus the actual data records each source yields.
endToEndExample.architecture: An abstract Source interface (abc.ABC) with concrete S3Source/PostgresSource; a Pipeline class composes a Source, a Transform, and a Sink (composition over inheritance). Dataclasses model immutable config; properties validate parameters; classmethods build pipelines from config.
processingSteps: 1. Define an abstract Source ABC with an abstract read() method so every source honors a common contract.
2. Implement S3Source and PostgresSource subclasses, each calling super().__init__ and providing read().
3. Model config as a frozen @dataclass with validated fields (via __post_init__ or property checks).
4. Build a Pipeline via Pipeline.from_config (a @classmethod) that composes the chosen source, transform, and sink.
5. Run the pipeline; __repr__ provides clear logging, and __eq__ enables idempotency/dedup checks.
endToEndExample.output: Transformed records written to the target sink, with each pipeline object self-describing in logs and configuration validated before any work begins.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Each component's __repr__ appears in structured logs; metrics track records processed per source. Property validation failures are logged as configuration errors before execution.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Validation happens in dataclass __post_init__ and property setters, failing fast on bad config. Abstract methods guarantee every source implements read(), so missing implementations fail at class definition/instantiation time, not at runtime mid-job.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A clean, extensible framework where adding a new source means writing one small subclass implementing the Source interface - no changes to Pipeline - demonstrating composition, polymorphism, and boilerplate-free dataclasses working together.

industryUseCases.problem: They must support many operator/asset types that share lifecycle behavior but differ in execution, and let users add custom ones easily.
industryUseCases.solution: Abstract base classes define the operator/asset interface; concrete operators subclass and override execute(); composition assembles tasks into DAGs. __repr__ aids debugging.
industryUseCases.benefits: Extensibility (users add operators by subclassing), consistent lifecycle, and clear, debuggable task objects.

industryUseCases.problem: Provide a uniform API across dozens of estimators/transformers while sharing fit/transform contracts and clean configuration.
industryUseCases.solution: A common base estimator class defines fit/transform; classmethods and properties expose parameters; composition (Pipeline) chains transformers. Dataclass-like config holds hyperparameters.
industryUseCases.benefits: Interchangeable components (polymorphism), composable pipelines, and consistent, well-documented interfaces.

industryUseCases.company: Cloud SDKs and Config Systems (e.g., AWS boto3, pydantic-based services)
industryUseCases.problem: Model API resources and configuration as typed objects with validation, equality, and safe immutable value types.
industryUseCases.solution: Dataclasses / typed models represent resources and config; properties and __post_init__ validate; frozen value objects are hashable for caching and dedup.
industryUseCases.benefits: Validated configuration, fewer runtime errors, and self-describing objects that integrate cleanly with caches and sets.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Favor composition and small interfaces so new behaviors are added by combining components rather than extending deep hierarchies; use __slots__ and lightweight dataclasses when instantiating millions of objects to control memory and GC pressure.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Keep __init__ side-effect-free (validate state, defer I/O to explicit methods) so objects can be safely constructed and reconstructed after failures; use factory classmethods that validate config and fail before resources are touched.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Design stateless or immutable (frozen) objects where possible so instances can be freely recreated across replicas without coordination; avoid shared mutable class attributes that act as hidden global state.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Make configuration objects serializable (dataclasses -> dict/JSON) so pipeline definitions can be persisted and rehydrated after an outage; ensure __eq__/__hash__ are stable for reliable dedup during replay.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: On hot paths prefer plain attribute access over properties, keep MRO shallow, and use __slots__ to avoid per-instance __dict__; dataclasses generate efficient methods comparable to hand-written code.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Reduce memory with __slots__ and immutable value objects, and avoid unnecessary object creation in tight loops; reuse instances or use namedtuples for simple records to cut allocation overhead.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Override __repr__ to redact secrets (passwords, tokens) so they don't leak into logs or tracebacks; use properties to validate and sanitize inputs rather than exposing raw mutable attributes.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Implement informative __repr__ for every domain object so logs and exceptions reveal state; expose key metrics (record counts, durations) via methods/properties for instrumentation.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Enforce invariants centrally in property setters and dataclass __post_init__ so invalid objects can never be constructed, catching data-quality issues at the boundary.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Use __repr__ in log messages for context, redact sensitive fields, and raise typed exceptions from validation so alerting can distinguish configuration errors from runtime failures.

recommendedPractices: **Prefer composition over inheritance:** model 'has-a' relationships by holding objects rather than deep subclassing.
**Use @dataclass for data-centric classes:** it removes boilerplate and gives correct __init__/__repr__/__eq__.
**Implement __repr__ for every class:** it makes objects debuggable in logs and tracebacks.
**Use @property for validation and computed values:** expose a clean attribute interface while enforcing invariants.
engineeringStandards: Always call super().__init__() in subclass initializers to properly initialize base state.
Never use mutable defaults (lists/dicts) as class attributes or default arguments; use default_factory or None + init.
When defining __eq__, also define __hash__ (or use frozen dataclass) so objects work in sets and dict keys.
designRecommendations: Keep hierarchies shallow; if you reach for the third level of inheritance, reconsider composition.
Define interfaces with abc.ABC / @abstractmethod (or typing.Protocol) so implementations are pluggable.
Keep __init__ free of I/O and heavy side effects; use classmethod factories for construction that can fail.
namingConventions: Use CapWords (PascalCase) for class names (ETLJob, S3Source).
Prefix non-public attributes/methods with a single underscore (self._row_count).
Use clear factory names like from_config / from_json for classmethod constructors.
documentationStandards: Give each class a docstring describing its responsibility and key invariants.
Document the public interface (which methods/properties callers should use) and which attributes are internal.
Document inheritance contracts: which methods subclasses must override (abstract methods).
testingStrategies: Test that __eq__ and __hash__ are consistent (equal objects hash equally; objects work in sets).
Test property setters reject invalid values (pytest.raises(ValueError)).
Test polymorphism by asserting subclasses honor the base interface, and test classmethod factories build the correct type.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a mutable default value (e.g., def __init__(self, items=[])).
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It looks intuitive and concise, and the bug only appears when the default is mutated across instances.
commonMistakes.impact: All instances share the same list/dict, so appends in one instance silently appear in others - a classic, hard-to-spot bug.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Default to None and create a new object in __init__ (items = items or []), or use field(default_factory=list) in a dataclass.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Inheritance feels like the obvious way to reuse code, and 'is-a' is conflated with 'shares code'.
commonMistakes.impact: Deep, rigid hierarchies (fragile base class problem), tight coupling, and surprising behavior from overridden methods and MRO.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Model 'has-a' relationships with composition; reserve inheritance for genuine subtype ('is-a') relationships and use ABCs/protocols for interfaces.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing @classmethod and @staticmethod (or forgetting to use cls).
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Both are decorators used inside classes and look similar; the role of cls vs no first argument is misunderstood.
commonMistakes.impact: A factory hardcoding the class name breaks subclassing; a staticmethod used where you needed class context fails to support inheritance.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use @classmethod (with cls) for factories/alternative constructors that should respect subclasses; use @staticmethod only for pure utilities needing no class/instance state.

comparisonSection.feature: Method type for utilities and factories
comparisonSection.explanation: @classmethod gets the class as cls, making it ideal for alternative constructors (from_dict, from_json) that should return the correct type even for subclasses. @staticmethod gets neither self nor cls and is just a function grouped in the class namespace - use it for pure helpers that need no class or instance state.

Composition builds behavior by holding other objects, giving loose coupling, easy testing (inject mocks), and runtime flexibility. Inheritance expresses true subtype relationships and enables polymorphism, but deep hierarchies become rigid (fragile base class) and tightly coupled. Prefer composition unless an 'is-a' relationship genuinely holds.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between an instance attribute and a class attribute?
beginnerQuestions.answer: An instance attribute is set on self (in __init__ or methods) and is unique to each object. A class attribute is defined in the class body and shared by all instances. If you read an attribute, Python checks the instance first, then the class; assigning to self.x always creates/updates an instance attribute.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: A great answer warns about mutable class attributes being shared across instances and shows the lookup order (instance then class).

beginnerQuestions.question: What does self represent and why is it the first parameter of methods?
beginnerQuestions.answer: self is the instance the method is called on. Python passes the instance automatically as the first argument, so obj.method() is really Class.method(obj). 'self' is just a convention for naming that parameter; it gives methods access to the instance's attributes and other methods.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Confirm they understand the bound-method mechanism (obj.method() -> Class.method(obj)) and that 'self' is convention, not a keyword.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between @classmethod and @staticmethod?
intermediateQuestions.answer: @classmethod receives the class as its first argument (cls) and is commonly used for alternative constructors/factories, since cls respects subclassing. @staticmethod receives neither self nor cls - it's a plain function namespaced in the class, used for utilities that don't need instance or class state. An instance method receives self.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Look for the from_dict factory example and the point that classmethods support subclassing via cls while a hardcoded class name wouldn't.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does super() work, and why call it in __init__?
intermediateQuestions.answer: super() returns a proxy that dispatches to the next class in the MRO (method resolution order). Calling super().__init__() runs the base class's initializer so inherited attributes are set up properly. In multiple inheritance, cooperative super() calls ensure every class in the MRO is initialized exactly once.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Strong answers mention the MRO and cooperative multiple inheritance, not just 'it calls the parent'.

intermediateQuestions.question: What does @dataclass give you, and how do you handle mutable defaults?
intermediateQuestions.answer: @dataclass auto-generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ from annotated fields. Options include frozen=True (immutable/hashable) and order=True (comparisons). For mutable defaults like lists you must use field(default_factory=list) instead of '= []', because a bare list would be shared across all instances.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Mention frozen for value objects/hashability and the default_factory requirement - both are common follow-ups.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain the MRO and how Python resolves methods in multiple inheritance.
advancedQuestions.answer: Python computes the MRO using C3 linearization, producing a consistent ordering of a class and all its bases. Attribute/method lookup follows this order, and super() dispatches to the next class in the MRO (not necessarily a direct parent). C3 guarantees that a class appears before its parents and respects the order bases are listed, raising an error if no consistent order exists (the diamond problem).
advancedQuestions.explanation: Mention the diamond problem and that super() is about the MRO, not literally 'the parent'. Knowing __mro__ exists is a plus.

advancedQuestions.question: When you define __eq__, what else must you consider, and why?
advancedQuestions.answer: Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None, making the object unhashable, so it can't be used in sets or as dict keys. You must define __hash__ consistently (objects that are equal must hash equally) or use @dataclass(frozen=True) which does this for you. You should also return NotImplemented for incomparable types so Python can try the reflected operation.
advancedQuestions.explanation: This tests the eq/hash contract. Bonus points for NotImplemented and for noting frozen dataclasses handle it automatically.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You're designing an ETL framework that must support new data sources (S3, Postgres, Kafka) added by other teams without modifying the core Pipeline code. How do you structure the classes?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Identify the stable abstraction: every source has a read() method. Define a contract (abstract base class or Protocol). Make Pipeline depend on that abstraction, not concrete sources. Use composition so Pipeline HAS-A source/transform/sink. Each new source is a small subclass implementing read(); Pipeline never changes (open/closed principle).
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Define an abstract Source class (abc.ABC) with an @abstractmethod read(). Implement concrete subclasses (S3Source, PostgresSource) that override read(). Pipeline composes a Source, Transform, and Sink and calls source.read() polymorphically. Adding Kafka means writing one KafkaSource subclass - no Pipeline changes - demonstrating composition plus polymorphism.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the object model for a configuration-driven data validation library where users declare rules (not-null, range, regex) and apply them to columns.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Define an abstract Rule with an @abstractmethod validate(value) -> bool and a message. Concrete rules (NotNullRule, RangeRule, RegexRule) subclass it. A ColumnValidator composes a list of Rules (composition). Rules and configs are immutable frozen dataclasses so they're hashable and safely shareable. Factory classmethods build rules from config dicts.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: ABCs give a clear contract but add ceremony; Protocols (structural typing) are lighter but less explicit. Frozen dataclasses ensure immutability/hashability at the cost of in-place mutation. Composition keeps the validator flexible but requires wiring rules together explicitly.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Make rules stateless and immutable so they can be reused across columns and run in parallel. Use __slots__ on hot objects, batch validation per column, and cache compiled regex in the rule's __init__. Serialize configs (dataclass -> dict) so rule sets can be stored and distributed to workers.

How do __slots__ improve memory usage and what are their limitations?
How does a @property differ from a plain attribute, and when is the overhead justified?
What is the diamond problem and how does Python's MRO resolve it?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Classes bundle state and behavior; Python OOP centers on __init__/self, inheritance with super(), dunder methods, properties, dataclasses, and composition over inheritance.
keyConcepts: Instance vs class attributes: per-object vs shared.
commands: class C:\n    def __init__(self, x):\n        self.x = x
interviewPoints: self is the instance; obj.m() == Class.m(obj).
classmethod gets cls (subclass-safe); staticmethod gets nothing.
super() follows the MRO, not literally the parent.
Defining __eq__ removes __hash__ - define it or use frozen dataclass.
quickNotes: Never use mutable defaults; use default_factory or None + init.
Implement __repr__ on every class for debuggability.
Use field(default_factory=list) for mutable dataclass fields.
Validate in property setters and dataclass __post_init__ to enforce invariants.
Use abc.ABC/@abstractmethod or typing.Protocol to define pluggable interfaces.

keyTakeaways: Classes bundle state and behavior: __init__ initializes per-instance attributes via self, while class attributes are shared across all instances (avoid mutable ones).
Use @classmethod (with cls) for subclass-safe factories and @staticmethod for pure utilities; instance methods take self and operate on object state.
Inheritance with super() enables polymorphism via the MRO, and dunder methods (__repr__, __eq__/__hash__) make objects debuggable and correctly comparable.
@property adds validation and computed attributes behind a clean interface, and @dataclass removes boilerplate (use frozen for immutable, hashable value objects).
Prefer composition (has-a) over deep inheritance (is-a) for flexible, testable designs, and define interfaces with abc.ABC or typing.Protocol for pluggable components.
